text:
A suspension bridge carries weight from its roadway to the earth through a continuous path of tension and compression. Everything begins on the deck, which supports both the dead load of its own structure and the live loads of vehicles, pedestrians, and wind. Beneath or integrated into this roadway is a stiffening girder or truss. Rather than allowing a heavy truck to cause a sharp local dip, this rigid framework spreads concentrated loads horizontally across a wider section of the span and helps the deck resist twisting in strong winds. Once distributed along the deck, the weight must move upward before it can reach the ground.

Attached at regular intervals along the edges of the deck are vertical suspender ropes, also called hangers. These slender steel cables are placed strictly in tension as the weight of the roadway pulls down on them. Acting like a row of taut vertical strings, the suspenders lift the load of the deck and deliver it to the sweeping main suspension cables draped high above. Because the deck’s weight is spread evenly across the horizontal length of the span, the main cables naturally hang in a parabolic curve. Each suspender adds its share of downward force to the main cables, which accumulate the entire weight of the suspended roadway along their length.

Inside the main cables, those vertical pulls transform into immense axial tension that runs along the curve of the steel wire bundles toward the two ends of the bridge. Because the cables slope upward as they approach the tall towers, the tensile force within them has both a vertical component and a horizontal component. At the top of each tower, the main cables rest inside heavy curved steel saddles. Here, the downward vertical component of the cable tension presses straight down on the tower tops, while the horizontal pulls from the main span and the side spans largely balance each other, preventing the towers from bending excessively sideways.

The towers themselves act as giant columns. They channel the downward force of the cables into massive compressive loads, carrying that tremendous weight straight down through their concrete or steel legs into deep foundations, caissons, or piers resting on solid bedrock beneath the water or soil. In this way, the vertical weight of the suspended roadway and cables is pushed directly into the earth.

However, the powerful horizontal pull carried along the main cables cannot simply stop at the towers; it continues down the backstays toward the land on either side of the bridge. At the ends of the structure, the main cables splay out and fasten securely inside massive concrete blocks called anchorages, or tunnel directly into solid rock cliffs. These anchorages resist the relentless upward and inward tug of the cables through sheer weight, friction against the soil, or deep rock anchoring. By transferring both the vertical compression through the towers and the horizontal tension into the anchorages, the suspension bridge safely grounds every pound of load from the deck into the earth.
